programs.title: The Green Planet
programs.desc:
The creators of the production invite viewers on a journey through the lush world of plants.It hides many surprising phenomena and hundreds of amazing heroes.Thanks to the lenses of specialized cameras, the mysterious life of nature's creations will be shown up close.Scientific research shows that nature is a perfect system of connecting vessels.In each of the five episodes, we will learn about a different group of plants and the secrets of their survival.The creators will talk about, among others:stories about seeds that can survive civilizations, trees that take care of each other, and creatures of nature that are as aggressive and spontaneous as animals.We will also learn about the relationships between people and animals with plants.It turns out that plants count, hunt, cheat, communicate, protect their relatives and manipulate animals for their own purposes.Contrary to appearances, when plants and animals interact with each other, it is usually the plant that sets the tone of the relationship.The series' narrator will be Sir David Attenborough, a popularizer of natural science
Viewers will discover the world of aquatic plants.They create some of the most beautiful and important habitats on Earth.Life in water is not easy, which is why individual plant species have found innovative ways to survive.The color-changing algae that grows on the Rainbow River in Colombia sticks to rocks thanks to a natural version of superglue.In the Brazilian Pantanal, plants fight for light using air bags.Their goal is to stay afloat and reproduce quickly.The globe seaweed, which comes from Japan, uses the water currents of Lake Akan to move to an ideal place for development.During the flowering period, aquatic plants behave like terrestrial plants for a time, displaying flowers into the air on stiff stems.Only one flowering plant has reached the sea and forms underwater communities - seagrass.Its submerged savannahs not only support large numbers of animals, but also sequester carbon dioxide 35 times faster than tropical forests.Now under threat, they are crucial in the fight against climate change.
